message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"1e6726c4fb675db06a952e0f7d7c4b2e7552a3b835bd6d4fe9dd1ff992d2ec49","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-va-class-std:lineage:72","source_registry_sha256":"b6300aba50e85a8fd509daf2f853e3d2d116b38a9707baf75df5057c8071f937","units":[{"unit_id":"sec04-u01","module_id":"sec04-m01","objective_ids":["sec04-u01"],"title":{"text":"Joints, junctions and curves","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Open and expansion joints are road surface hazards, and junction signs tell you how the road ahead meets another.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04"]},{"text":"Curve signs tell you to slow and prepare, and a posted safe speed tells you how much.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Lia approaches a T intersection sign on a country road.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A T intersection ends your road at a stop sign, where you must turn after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},"result":{"text":"Lia plans to stop at the stop sign, yield, and then turn right or left.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: treating a T intersection like a Y and bearing through without stopping.","fact_ids":["sec04-R04"]},"correction":{"text":"A Y junction only forks your path right or left, while a T junction ends your road at a stop sign with a forced turn and yield.","fact_ids":["sec04-R04","sec04-F04"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Y bears; T stops and turns.","fact_ids":["sec04-R04"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Lia reaches the end of her road at a T intersection. What must she do?","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]},"answer":{"text":"Stop at the stop sign, yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, then turn.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},"rationale":{"text":"A T intersection ends your road at a stop sign with a forced turn and yield, unlike a Y, which only forks your path.","fact_ids":["sec04-R04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Reading the road ahead","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Open and expansion joints.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},{"text":"Intersection, Y, T and roundabout signs.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},{"text":"Curve and turn warnings.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Welcome to the first lesson of this section. Before the railroad crossings and work zones, we look at warning signs and road features that describe the road just ahead of you. Open joints on bridges or ramps can throw a motorcyclist, and expansion joints bump traffic or cost traction in wet weather. Then come the junction signs: the plain intersection warning, the Y and the T intersections, and the roundabout sign. Finally we cover the curve and turn warnings, from a right curve with a side road to sharp turns, reverse curves, safe speed indicators and the winding road. Each one tells you how to prepare before you reach it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Joints and junctions","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Open joints can throw a motorcyclist.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F06"]},{"text":"Expansion joints: bumps, wet traction loss.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F06"]},{"text":"Intersection sign: watch for entering vehicles.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Start with the road surface. Open joints on bridges or ramps can throw a motorcyclist, so slow down for them. Expansion joints bump traffic or cost traction in wet weather where they span the lanes. Now the first junction sign. An intersection warning sign means a junction is ahead, so stay alert for vehicles entering your road. A right curve with a side road sign means the road bends right while a side road joins from the left inside the curve, and again the instruction is to watch for entering vehicles. In both cases, the sign gives you time to look for other traffic before it appears in front of you.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Y is not T","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Y: bear right or left.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},{"text":"T: your road ends at a stop sign.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},{"text":"Turn after yielding.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. A Y intersection and a T intersection both show a road splitting, but they ask very different things of you. A Y intersection forces a right or left bear ahead. A T intersection ends your road at a stop sign, where you must turn after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. So a Y junction only forks your path right or left, while a T junction ends your road at a stop sign with a forced turn and yield. If you treat a T like a Y and keep rolling, you will miss the stop sign at the end of your road. The memory line for this slide is short: Y bears, and T stops and turns.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":48,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Roundabout signs","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Circular intersection with a center island.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F04"]},{"text":"One or more lanes.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F04"]},{"text":"Yield to the circle; travel counterclockwise.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Roundabout signs announce a circular intersection with a center island and one or more lanes. Entering traffic yields to traffic already in the circle, and all traffic travels counterclockwise. Those two rules, yield on entry and travel counterclockwise, are the core of the roundabout sign's message. The number of lanes may vary, but the yielding rule and the direction of travel do not. Compare the T intersection from the last slide: at a T you stop at a stop sign and turn, while at a roundabout you yield to the circle as you enter. So the roundabout sign tells you two things to do before you reach the circle: yield on entry, then travel counterclockwise.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Curves and turns","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Sharp turns and reverse curves: slow and prepare.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},{"text":"Safe speed indicator: slow to the posted speed.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},{"text":"Winding road: slow on every curve.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Sharp right turns, sharp right-then-left turns, and right-then-left curves each demand slowing and full preparation for the bend. A right curve with a safe speed indicator means slowing to that posted speed. A winding road sign, with its series of turns, means slowing on every curve for control. So single sharp turns and double sharp turns each warn of one hard bend sequence, while winding road warns of a whole series of curves. When a safe speed is posted with the curve sign, that posted speed is your target for the curve. On a winding road, the instruction applies to every curve in the series, not just the first one you meet.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the junction","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Your road ends at a T.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},{"text":"What must you do?","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Lia is driving on a country road and reaches the end of her road at a T intersection. What must she do? Work it out before reading on. The answer: stop at the stop sign, yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, and then turn. A T intersection ends your road at a stop sign, where you must turn after yielding. If Lia were at a Y intersection instead, she would bear right or left, because a Y junction only forks the path. The T is the one with the stop sign and the forced turn. If you answered that she could bear through without stopping, you were describing the Y, not the T.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":47,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Road-ahead recap","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Slow for joints.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},{"text":"Y bears, T stops and turns.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},{"text":"Slow for every posted curve.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close the lesson: slow down for open joints, which can throw a motorcyclist, and for expansion joints, which bump traffic or cost wet traction. An intersection sign means watch for entering vehicles, and so does a right curve with a side road. A Y forces a right or left bear, while a T ends your road at a stop sign with a turn after yielding. At a roundabout, entering traffic yields to the circle and travels counterclockwise. Sharp turns and reverse curves demand slowing and preparation, a safe speed indicator means slow to the posted speed, and a winding road means slow on every curve. Next, railroad crossings.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec04-u02","module_id":"sec04-m02","objective_ids":["sec04-u02"],"title":{"text":"Railroad crossing signs and signals","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R05","sec04-F10"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Advance signs warn you early, and the crossbuck marks the crossing itself, where trains may come from either direction.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-R02"]},{"text":"Flashing lights and gates turn readiness to stop into a required stop and wait.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Max stops at a crossing with flashing lights, and one train passes.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12"]},"reasoning":{"text":"You wait until every train or rail vehicle has passed, the tracks are clear and the lights stop, watching for a second train from the opposite way.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]},"result":{"text":"Max keeps waiting until the lights stop and the tracks are clear.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: going as soon as the first train clears while the lights still flash.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12"]},"correction":{"text":"Flashing lights command a full stop until all trains have passed, the tracks are clear and the lights stop, because a second train may come from the opposite way.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R01","sec04-R03"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Crossbuck ready, lights stop, gates wait.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"One train has passed, but the crossing lights are still flashing. May Max go?","fact_ids":["sec04-F12"]},"answer":{"text":"No. He waits until every train has passed, the tracks are clear and the lights stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R01"]},"rationale":{"text":"Flashing lights command a full stop until all is clear, and a second train may come from the opposite way.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-R03"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Approaching the rails","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14","sec04-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Low ground and advance signs.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14","sec04-R01"]},{"text":"Crossbuck, lights and gates.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14","sec04-R01"]},{"text":"Pavement marking.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14","sec04-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Welcome to the lesson on railroad crossing signs and signals. Crossings use a series of warnings, starting well before the tracks and ending at the rails themselves. We will cover the low ground crossing sign, the advance warning signs, the crossbuck, flashing lights, gates and the X with RR painted on some approaches. The most important idea in this lesson is that each device asks a little more of you than the one before it. A crossbuck alone asks you to be ready to stop. Flashing lights require a full stop until everything is clear. Gates hold you until they rise. We will build up to that contrast one device at a time.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14","sec04-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Low ground and advance signs","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R05","sec04-F10","sec04-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"Low ground: steep slope can hang a low vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R05","sec04-F10","sec04-F14"]},{"text":"Advance signs: look, listen, slow, be ready to stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R05","sec04-F10","sec04-F14"]},{"text":"Pavement X with RR on some approaches.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R05","sec04-F10","sec04-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"A low ground railroad crossing sign warns that a steep slope can hang a low vehicle on the tracks. Compare that with the road joints in the last lesson: low ground crossings threaten to hang low vehicles on the rails, while open and expansion joints threaten motorcycle control and wet traction. Advance railroad crossing signs tell you to look, listen, slow down, and stand ready to stop for trains or any rail vehicles. And on some approaches, an X with RR painted on the pavement may mark the way to the crossing. These early warnings come before the crossbuck, which marks the crossing itself.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R05","sec04-F10","sec04-F14"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The crossbuck","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-R02","sec04-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Marks the crossing itself.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-R02","sec04-R03"]},{"text":"Look, listen, slow, prepare to stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-R02","sec04-R03"]},{"text":"Trains from either direction, on either track.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-R02","sec04-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"A crossbuck warns of the crossing itself. Look, listen, slow and prepare to stop, since trains may come from either direction, and at multi-track crossings, from either track. Advance crossing signs upstream ask for looking, listening and slowing, while the crossbuck at the rails marks the decision point itself. The number of tracks matters. One track threatens trains from either direction, while multiple tracks threaten either direction on either track, plus a second train from the opposite way. So at a crossbuck with several tracks, checking once in each direction is not enough: each track can bring a train from either side.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-R02","sec04-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Flashing lights and gates","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Lights: stop when flashing starts.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]},{"text":"Wait for all trains, clear tracks, lights off.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]},{"text":"Gates: stay stopped until they rise; never drive around.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Where flashing lights join the crossbuck, stop when the flashing starts. Wait until every train or rail vehicle has passed, the tracks are clear, and the lights stop, watching for a second train from the opposite way. Where gates join the lights, stop when the flashing starts, before the gate falls. Stay stopped until the gates rise and the lights stop. And never drive around a lowered gate. So the three devices form a ladder. A lone crossbuck asks readiness to stop, flashing lights command a full stop until all is clear, and gates hold you until they rise. The higher the device on the ladder, the stronger the rule it gives you.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"One train is not all","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Lights still flashing: keep waiting.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]},{"text":"Watch for a second train.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]},{"text":"Go only when lights stop and tracks are clear.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. A train passes, the crossing looks open, and a driver starts to go while the lights are still flashing. The rule says otherwise. At flashing lights you wait until every train or rail vehicle has passed, the tracks are clear, and the lights stop, watching for a second train from the opposite way. At multi-track crossings, multiple tracks threaten either direction on either track plus a second train from the opposite way. So the end of one train is not the end of the danger, and it is not the end of your wait. The lights stopping, together with clear tracks, is your signal to go, not the last car of the first train.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":47,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the lights","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R01","sec04-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"One train has passed.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R01","sec04-F13"]},{"text":"Lights still flashing.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R01","sec04-F13"]},{"text":"Go or wait?","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R01","sec04-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Max is stopped at a crossing with flashing lights. One train passes, and the lights are still flashing. May he go? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Where flashing lights join the crossbuck, you wait until every train or rail vehicle has passed, the tracks are clear, and the lights stop, watching for a second train from the opposite way. Max keeps waiting. Flashing lights command a full stop until all is clear, and if gates were also present, he would stay stopped until the gates rise and the lights stop, and never drive around a lowered gate.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R01","sec04-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Crossing device ladder","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F14","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Crossbuck: be ready to stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F14","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]},{"text":"Lights: stop until all is clear.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F14","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]},{"text":"Gates: wait until they rise.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F14","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close the lesson: a low ground crossing sign warns that a steep slope can hang a low vehicle on the tracks. Advance signs tell you to look, listen, slow down and be ready to stop, and an X with RR on the pavement may mark the approach. The crossbuck marks the crossing itself, where trains may come from either direction and, at multi-track crossings, from either track. Flashing lights mean stop and wait until every train has passed, the tracks are clear and the lights stop. Gates mean stay stopped until they rise, and never drive around a lowered gate. The memory line: crossbuck ready, lights stop, gates wait.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F14","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec04-u03","module_id":"sec04-m03","objective_ids":["sec04-u03"],"title":{"text":"Crossing safety and emergencies","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F18","sec04-R07"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Trains can reach a crossing at any time from either direction, so you never start across without room to clear.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15"]},{"text":"The manual gives specific actions for a stalled car, for school buses and for reporting a dangerous crossing.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18","sec04-F16","sec04-F17"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Kai's car stalls on the tracks.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18"]},"reasoning":{"text":"If your car stalls on the tracks, get out at once and run diagonally away from the tracks in the direction of the oncoming train.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18","sec04-R07"]},"result":{"text":"Kai leaves the car right away and runs diagonally away from the tracks toward the direction the train is coming from.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: staying in a stalled car on the tracks to try restarting it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18"]},"correction":{"text":"A stalled car must be abandoned at once for a diagonal run away from the tracks toward the train side.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18","sec04-R07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Stalled: out and diagonal, toward the train.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Kai's car stalls on the tracks and a train is coming. Which way should he run?","fact_ids":["sec04-F18"]},"answer":{"text":"Diagonally away from the tracks, in the direction of the oncoming train.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18","sec04-R07"]},"rationale":{"text":"The manual says get out at once and run diagonally away from the tracks in the direction of the oncoming train.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Safe crossing habits","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F18","sec04-F16","sec04-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"Clear the tracks completely.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F18","sec04-F16","sec04-F17"]},{"text":"Stalled car: get out.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F18","sec04-F16","sec04-F17"]},{"text":"Buses and emergency signs.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F18","sec04-F16","sec04-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"Welcome to the lesson on crossing safety and emergencies. The signs and signals from the last lesson tell you when a train is coming. This lesson covers what you must do to stay safe at any crossing, and what to do when something goes wrong. Trains can reach a crossing at any time from either direction, so the first rule is about room on the far side of the tracks. Then we cover what to do if your car stalls on the tracks, the rule that school buses always stop at railroad crossings, and how to report a dangerous condition at a crossing using the emergency sign posted there. Each rule is short, and each is worth knowing exactly.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F18","sec04-F16","sec04-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":48,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Room on the far side","fact_ids":["sec04-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Trains can come at any time, from either direction.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15"]},{"text":"Never start across unless you can clear completely.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15"]},{"text":"Room must be waiting beyond the tracks.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"Trains can reach a crossing at any time from either direction. So never start across unless you can clear the tracks completely, with room waiting on the far side. Because a train can come at any time, this rule does not depend on lights or gates. If there is no room for your car beyond the rails, the rule tells you not to start across. The test is simple. Before you move onto the tracks, ask whether your whole vehicle can get across and off them with space to spare. If the answer is no, you wait before the crossing until there is room.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Entering versus stalled","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F18","sec04-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Moving car: never enter without a clear exit.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F18","sec04-R07"]},{"text":"Stalled car: get out at once.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F18","sec04-R07"]},{"text":"Run diagonally toward the train's direction.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F18","sec04-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap: the two situations call for opposite thinking about your car. A moving car must never enter the crossing without a guaranteed clear exit. But if your car stalls on the tracks, the car no longer matters.
